title: 15 — API Design
html:
15 — API Design

An API is a contract, and contracts are expensive to change. Everything below is about making the contract obvious to consumers, cheap to evolve, and hard to misuse.

1. Choosing the style

Style Transport Shape Best for Weak at
REST/HTTP+JSON HTTP/1.1, 2 Resources + verbs Public APIs, CRUD, broad client support, caching Chatty for graphs; over/under-fetching
gRPC HTTP/2, protobuf Typed RPC, streaming Service-to-service, low latency, high throughput, polyglot Browser needs a proxy; binary is harder to debug
GraphQL HTTP POST Client-specified query Many clients with divergent data needs; mobile bandwidth Caching, rate limiting, query-cost control, N+1
Webhooks HTTP callbacks Push to the consumer Notifying third parties Delivery reliability, security, retries
WebSocket/SignalR Persistent Bi-directional Live updates, collaboration Statefulness, scale-out
Async messaging Broker Events/commands Decoupling, long work Not request/response (file 14)

Default: REST for public and general-purpose APIs; gRPC for internal service-to-service where you control both ends; GraphQL only when the "many clients, many shapes" problem is real and you're prepared to own query-cost limiting and dataloader batching.

2. REST done properly

2.1 Resource modelling

/portfolios                          collection
/portfolios/{id}                     item
/portfolios/{id}/holdings            sub-collection
/portfolios/{id}/holdings/{hid}      sub-item
/portfolios/{id}:rebalance           an action that isn't CRUD (or POST /rebalances)

Rules: plural nouns, lowercase, hyphens not underscores, no verbs in paths, no file extensions, no trailing slash. Nest at most one level — beyond that, use query parameters (/holdings?portfolioId=42) or the resource's own top-level path.

Non-CRUD actions are the standard awkwardness. Options, best first:

  1. Model the action as a resource: POST /portfolios/42/rebalances returns a rebalance resource you can poll. Naturally async, auditable, retryable.
  2. A sub-resource for state: PUT /orders/42/status {"status":"cancelled"}.
  3. A controller-style path as a last resort: POST /orders/42:cancel.

2.2 Methods and their contracts

Method Safe Idempotent Body Use
GET ✔ ✔ ✘ Retrieve. Never mutate — crawlers, prefetchers, and retries will hit it
HEAD ✔ ✔ ✘ Metadata only
POST ✘ ✘ ✔ Create, or non-idempotent actions
PUT ✘ ✔ ✔ Full replace (or create at a client-chosen id)
PATCH ✘ ✘* ✔ Partial update (*idempotent if you use JSON Merge Patch with absolute values)
DELETE ✘ ✔ ✘ Remove. Second call → 404 or 204, be consistent

Idempotency is a contract, not a suggestion. Any client, proxy, or retry policy is entitled to repeat a GET/PUT/DELETE. Design accordingly.

2.3 Status codes

Use the table in 01_NETWORKING_FUNDAMENTALS §6.1. The distinctions that matter most in practice:

  • 400 vs 422 — can't parse vs parsed-but-invalid.
  • 401 vs 403 — not authenticated vs not permitted.
  • 404 vs 403 — for resources the caller may not even know exist, return 404 to avoid leaking existence.
  • 409 — conflict (duplicate, concurrent modification).
  • 412 — precondition failed (optimistic concurrency via If-Match).
  • 202 — accepted for async processing; include a status URL.
  • 429 — always with Retry-After.

2.4 Errors: use RFC 9457 Problem Details

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-balance",
  "title": "Insufficient balance",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Account GB29 has a balance of 40.00 GBP; the transfer requires 100.00 GBP.",
  "instance": "/transfers/8f2c",
  "traceId": "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01",
  "errors": {
    "amount": ["Amount exceeds the available balance."]
  }
}

// ASP.NET Core: consistent problem responses for everything, including unhandled exceptions
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails(options =>
{
    options.CustomizeProblemDetails = ctx =>
    {
        ctx.ProblemDetails.Extensions["traceId"] = Activity.Current?.Id ?? ctx.HttpContext.TraceIdentifier;
        ctx.ProblemDetails.Instance = ctx.HttpContext.Request.Path;
    };
});
app.UseExceptionHandler();       // maps unhandled exceptions to ProblemDetails
app.UseStatusCodePages();

Error design rules:

  • A stable, machine-readable code (type or an code field) — clients must not parse English.
  • Actionable detail: what was wrong and what to do. Not "An error occurred".
  • Include the trace id so a support ticket maps to a log entry in one search.
  • Never leak internals — stack traces, SQL, file paths, or internal hostnames in a client-facing error is an information-disclosure vulnerability.
  • Field-level errors for validation, keyed by the request field path.

2.5 Pagination, filtering, sorting

GET /trades?portfolioId=42&status=settled&from=2026-01-01
          &sort=-tradeDate,instrumentCode
          &limit=50&cursor=eyJkIjoiMjAyNi0wNy0yMCIsImkiOjkxMn0

{
  "data": [ ... ],
  "pagination": {
    "limit": 50,
    "nextCursor": "eyJkIjoiMjAyNi0wNy0xOSIsImkiOjg4MX0",
    "hasMore": true
  }
}
Offset (?page=3&size=50) Cursor/keyset
Deep pages Degrades linearly Constant cost
Stability Items shift between pages as data changes Stable
Jump to page N ✔ ✘
Total count Easy (but expensive) Usually omitted

Recommendation: cursor pagination for anything large or real-time; offset only where users genuinely need page numbers, and cap the maximum offset. Always enforce a maximum limit (e.g. 100) — an unbounded limit=1000000 is a DoS.

Filtering: keep it simple and explicit (status=settled&minNotional=1000). Resist building a query language in query strings; if consumers need that, you actually need a reporting endpoint or GraphQL.

2.6 Payload conventions

Rule Detail
Casing Pick one (camelCase is the JSON norm) and never mix
Dates ISO 8601 UTC with offset: 2026-07-27T14:30:00Z. Never dd/MM/yyyy, never a bare local time
Money {"amount": "1234.56", "currency": "GBP"} — string or minor-unit integer, never a float
Enums Strings ("settled"), not integers — readable and stable across versions
Booleans Name them positively (isActive, not isNotDisabled)
Nulls Be consistent: omit or null, don't mix. Document which
IDs Opaque strings to the client; don't expose sequential internal IDs if enumeration matters
Envelopes Either always wrap ({"data": ...}) or never. Consistency beats the debate
Collections Always an object at the top level, never a bare array (leaves room for pagination metadata, and avoids a legacy JSON hijacking issue)

2.7 Idempotency for POST

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 8f2c1a4e-...     (client-generated, unique per logical operation)

Server: store the key with the response; on a repeat, return the original response without re-executing. Key expiry ~24 h. This is what makes client retries safe, and it's mandatory for anything involving money.

public async Task<IActionResult> CreatePayment(
    [FromHeader(Name = "Idempotency-Key")] string idempotencyKey,
    CreatePaymentRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(idempotencyKey))
        return Problem(statusCode: 400, title: "Idempotency-Key header is required.");

    var existing = await _idempotency.TryGetAsync(idempotencyKey, ct);
    if (existing is not null)
    {
        // Same key, different body = a client bug. Fail loudly rather than silently returning the old result.
        if (existing.RequestHash != Hash(request))
            return Problem(statusCode: 422, title: "Idempotency-Key reused with a different payload.");
        return StatusCode(existing.StatusCode, existing.Body);
    }
    ...
}

2.8 Concurrency control

GET  /portfolios/42        → 200, ETag: "v17"
PUT  /portfolios/42        If-Match: "v17"
                           → 200 (applied) or 412 Precondition Failed (someone else changed it)

This is optimistic concurrency at the HTTP layer, backed by a rowversion column. Without it, last-write-wins silently discards other users' edits — a data-loss bug that users experience as "the system lost my changes".

2.9 Long-running operations

POST /reports                → 202 Accepted
                               Location: /reports/8f2c
                               Retry-After: 5
GET  /reports/8f2c           → 200 {"status":"running","progress":0.4}
                             → 200 {"status":"succeeded","resultUrl":"https://..."}
                             → 200 {"status":"failed","error":{...}}

Never hold an HTTP request open for minutes. Either poll (above), push (SignalR/WebSocket), or callback (webhook).

3. Versioning

Strategy Example Pros Cons
URI path /v1/portfolios Obvious, cacheable, easy to route Not "pure REST"; duplicates routes
Header Api-Version: 2026-07-01 Clean URLs Invisible in logs/browsers; harder to test
Media type Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json Correct per HTTP spec Awkward for most clients
Query string ?api-version=2.0 Simple Pollutes URLs, easy to omit
Date-based Api-Version: 2026-07-01 (Stripe-style) Fine-grained, per-consumer pinning Requires transformation layers

Recommendation: URI path versioning for major versions (/v1, /v2), with strict additive-only evolution within a version.

Non-breaking (safe within a version): adding an endpoint, adding an optional request field, adding a response field, adding a new enum value only if clients were told to tolerate unknown values, relaxing a validation rule. Breaking (needs a new version): removing/renaming a field, changing a type or format, making an optional field required, changing status codes or error shapes, tightening validation, changing default behaviour.

⚠️ Adding an enum value is breaking for strictly-typed clients. Document from day one: "clients must ignore unknown enum values and unknown fields" (Postel's law, applied deliberately).

Deprecation process: announce → Deprecation and Sunset headers + docs → monitor per-consumer usage → contact remaining users → remove. Never remove silently. Support at most two major versions concurrently or the maintenance burden compounds.

4. gRPC

syntax = "proto3";
package portfolio.v1;

service PortfolioService {
  rpc GetPortfolio (GetPortfolioRequest) returns (Portfolio);
  rpc ListHoldings (ListHoldingsRequest) returns (stream Holding);      // server streaming
  rpc WatchPrices  (stream PriceRequest) returns (stream PriceUpdate);  // bidirectional
}

message GetPortfolioRequest { string portfolio_id = 1; }

message Portfolio {
  string portfolio_id = 1;
  string name         = 2;
  repeated Holding holdings = 3;
  // field 4 was `legacy_code`, removed in v1.3 — never reuse a field number
  reserved 4;
  reserved "legacy_code";
}

Rules: field numbers are the wire contract — never renumber or reuse; adding a field is safe; removing one requires reserved. Use proto3 optional/wrapper types when you must distinguish "absent" from "zero" (a real source of bugs: int32 quantity = 1 cannot tell 0 from unset).

Why gRPC internally: ~5–10× smaller payloads than JSON, generated clients in every language, HTTP/2 multiplexing, first-class streaming, deadlines built into the protocol. Costs: needs h2 end-to-end (load balancers must support it; L4 LBs pin all calls to one backend because h2 multiplexes on one connection — use client-side load balancing or a mesh); not directly browser-callable (gRPC-Web + proxy); binary payloads are harder to inspect.

Deadlines, not timeouts: gRPC propagates a deadline down the call chain, so a downstream service knows how long the original caller is still waiting. Always set one:

var reply = await client.GetPortfolioAsync(request, deadline: DateTime.UtcNow.AddSeconds(5));

5. GraphQL

The genuine wins: one round trip for a nested view; each client fetches exactly the fields it needs; a strongly-typed, introspectable schema; no version proliferation (deprecate fields instead).

The costs you must plan for:

Problem Mitigation
N+1 resolvers DataLoader batching per request — not optional, it's the difference between working and unusable
Unbounded query cost Depth limit, complexity/cost analysis, persisted queries, pagination enforced in the schema
HTTP caching is lost POST + arbitrary bodies; use persisted queries + CDN, or APQ, or accept app-level caching only
Authorisation Must be enforced per field/resolver, not per endpoint — a much larger surface
Rate limiting Per-request limits are meaningless; limit by query cost
Error semantics Always HTTP 200 with an errors array — monitoring must look inside the body

Recommendation: use GraphQL when you have several clients with genuinely divergent data needs and a team that will own the schema. Don't use it as "a nicer REST" for a single Angular app — you inherit all the costs and few of the benefits.

6. Webhooks (you as the provider)

POST https://customer.example.com/hooks/trades
X-Webhook-Id: 8f2c1a4e
X-Webhook-Timestamp: 1785412345
X-Webhook-Signature: sha256=9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31
Content-Type: application/json

Provider obligations:

  • Sign the payload (HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp + body with a per-subscriber secret) and document verification. Include the timestamp and require the receiver to reject old ones (replay protection).
  • Retry with exponential backoff over hours; then disable the endpoint and notify.
  • At-least-once delivery → include a unique event id so receivers can dedupe.
  • Fast timeout (5–10 s) — receivers should ack and process async.
  • Provide a replay/redelivery UI and a delivery log.
  • Support endpoint rotation and secret rotation with two valid secrets during the overlap.

Consumer obligations (when you receive webhooks): verify the signature before parsing; return 2xx immediately and queue the work; dedupe by event id; never trust the payload's contents over your own source of truth (re-fetch for anything security- or money-relevant).

7. Cross-cutting API concerns

Concern Do
AuthN OAuth2/OIDC bearer tokens; API keys only for server-to-server, scoped and rotatable
AuthZ Per-resource, server-side, deny-by-default (file 13 §3 A01)
Rate limiting Per identity, documented, with 429 + Retry-After + X-RateLimit-* headers
Payload limits Max body size at the proxy and the app; max array lengths; max page size
Timeouts Server-side request timeout; documented client guidance
Compression gzip/br on responses > ~1 KB
Caching Cache-Control, ETag, Vary — file 01 §6.2
CORS Explicit allow-list, never reflect the Origin header
Correlation Accept and echo X-Correlation-Id/traceparent; include it in every error
Content negotiation JSON default; only add formats you'll actually maintain
HATEOAS Rarely worth the cost; a pragmatic middle ground is including next/self links in pagination

8. Documentation & contracts

OpenAPI is the artifact, not the afterthought. Generate it from code (annotations + XML docs) or write it first (design-first) — either works, but it must be accurate, versioned, and published in CI.

app.MapGet("/portfolios/{id:int}", GetPortfolio)
   .WithName("GetPortfolio")
   .WithSummary("Retrieve a portfolio by id")
   .WithDescription("Returns the portfolio header and its current holdings as of the last business day.")
   .Produces<PortfolioResponse>(StatusCodes.Status200OK)
   .ProducesProblem(StatusCodes.Status404NotFound)
   .ProducesProblem(StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden)
   .RequireAuthorization("PortfolioRead");

A good API doc includes, beyond the schema: authentication setup, a working curl example per endpoint, error codes and what to do about each, rate limits, pagination semantics, idempotency guidance, versioning/deprecation policy, a changelog, and sandbox credentials.

Contract testing stops the "we changed the API and didn't know who broke" problem:

  • Provider-side: OpenAPI diff in CI, failing the build on a breaking change.
  • Consumer-driven contracts (Pact): each consumer publishes its expectations; the provider verifies against all of them before deploying.
  • Schema registry for message contracts (file 14 §8).

9. Performance

Technique Effect
Right-size payloads Don't return 60 fields when the client uses 6. Add sparse fieldsets (?fields=id,name) if clients differ
Avoid N+1 at the API layer One endpoint that returns the aggregate beats five round trips
Batch endpoints POST /trades/batch-get {"ids":[...]} for clients that need many items
Compression 60–80% reduction on JSON
HTTP caching ETag + 304 avoids the payload entirely
Connection reuse Keep-alive, HTTP/2 (file 01 §3.1)
Streaming IAsyncEnumerable + chunked responses for large result sets — first byte fast, constant memory
Pagination enforced Never allow an unbounded result set
Async for slow work 202 + polling, not a 4-minute request

Set and publish a latency budget per endpoint (e.g. p99 < 300 ms) and alert on it. An API without a stated performance contract degrades one PR at a time.

10. Checklist & interview angles

API review checklist

  • Resources are nouns; actions modelled as resources or sub-resources
  • Correct method semantics; GET is safe; PUT/DELETE idempotent
  • Status codes precise; 401 vs 403 vs 404 deliberate
  • Errors use Problem Details with a stable machine-readable code and a trace id
  • No internal details leaked in errors
  • Pagination on every collection, with a maximum page size
  • Filtering/sorting fields allow-listed (SQL-injection and index-abuse defence)
  • Idempotency-Key on non-idempotent mutations that matter
  • ETag/If-Match for concurrent updates
  • Consistent casing, ISO 8601 UTC dates, money as decimal-string or minor units
  • Versioning strategy documented; changes additive within a version
  • AuthN/AuthZ enforced server-side per resource
  • Rate limits documented and returned in headers
  • Request size limits and timeouts configured
  • OpenAPI accurate, published, and diffed in CI
  • Correlation ID accepted, propagated, and returned
  • Long-running operations use 202 + status resource

🔍 Interview angles

  • PUT vs PATCH vs POST? Full replace (idempotent) vs partial update vs create/non-idempotent action.
  • How do you make POST safe to retry? Client-supplied Idempotency-Key, stored with the original response; repeats return the stored result.
  • How do you version an API without breaking clients? Additive-only within a version, URI path for majors, deprecation headers with a sunset date, and monitoring per-consumer usage before removal.
  • REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL? Answer by consumer and constraint: public/broad → REST; internal, typed, high-throughput → gRPC; many clients with divergent shapes → GraphQL (and name the DataLoader/cost-limiting cost).
  • How do you prevent one client from degrading the API for everyone? Per-identity rate limits, payload and page-size caps, query timeouts, bulkheads, and load shedding at the gateway.
  • Two users edit the same record concurrently. What happens? ETag + If-Match → 412 for the loser, with a UI that shows the conflict. Last-write-wins is a silent data-loss bug.
  • Where do you put business logic in an API? Not in the controller — the controller maps HTTP to a use case and back. That keeps the logic testable and reusable from a worker or CLI.
